heading: Five families, some unplaced households, and a lot of namesakes
lead: This site has been counting badly. It said «seven lines», then «eight», and listed Senj beside Carnia as though they were the same kind of thing — when Senj is a place our own family reached and Carnia is where it started. Three different things were being added together. They are separated here, and the count only applies to the first of them — which now runs to five, because Corsica has earned a lane of its own.

why.text: Four households of the surname can be traced to a place they came *from*, and they came from three different directions for three different reasons. Three are documented; the fourth is family lore. **These are the only things this archive calls families**, and nothing joins any two of them.

why.lab: A station is not a family
why.text: Gologorica, Gračišće, Crikvenica, Senj, Pfullingen are **stops on one road** — our road — not separate lines. So are Perinuša and Opačac on the Venetian road, and Umag, Brtonigla and Koper on the Cretan one. They have pages because there is a lot to say about each; they are not additions to the count.

why.lab: And a line can run beside ours without being ours
why.text: **Corsica is the clearest case, and it is now drawn as a line rather than buried in a footnote.** It has everything the other four have — a place, a first generation with dates, six documented generations, a route out and a diaspora — and it has no connection to Istria whatever. That is exactly why it is worth drawing. A reader who finds a Franceschi in Puerto Rico or Caracas should be able to see, on the same picture, that there is a fully documented family of the name that goes there and is not this one.

why.lab: And a namesake is not a relative
why.text: *De Franceschi* means only «of the Franceschi» — the household of a man called Francesco. It was invented independently wherever an Italian-speaking clerk had two Francescos to tell apart. So a De Franceschi in Corsica or Bologna or Rio Grande do Sul is not evidence of anything at all until a document joins them, and this archive will not pretend otherwise.

families.name: Out of Carnia, for work
families.from: The Val di Gorto above Ovaro, in Friuli
families.rests: A De Franceschi of Mione on the 1679 headmen's list, working in the County of Pazin; the surname in the Moncalvo di Pisino baptism book from 1661; ANNO · DOMNI · 1711 cut over the house at Gologorica; and an unbroken register descent at Gračišće from 1787.
families.who: This archive's own family, and Carlo and Camillo De Franceschi's.

families.name: Out of Venice, as soldiers
families.from: Venice, by way of Zadar and Omiš
families.rests: Louis I's privilege of 1359; the foundation plaque of Francesco the Venetian at Omiš dated 18 June 1584; Provveditore Mocenigo's donation charter of 1717; the Imotski death register of 1845, where a Franceschi born at Omiš dies at Imotski.
families.who: Zuane, who took Imotski in 1717, and the mills at Perinuša.

families.name: Out of Crete, as refugees
families.from: Candia, by way of Zante and Šibenik
families.rests: The Venetian war pension of 1674, still being drawn at Capodistria in 1730; Chrysoula Marulli, a Cretan wife married in 1727; and the estate at Seget bought in 1720 with 1724 on its portal and 1732 on its cistern. The flight itself is tradition, well supported.
families.who: The Seget and Umag house, nobles of Capodistria from 1802.

families.name: Southern Istria — Pula, Fažana, Ližnjan
families.from: Unknown — but a Friulian trace at Zoppola
families.rests: Thirty-one people in the family's own tree, in the Pula and Fažana registers from **1667** and at Ližnjan into the twentieth century. **This is now known to be the tail of a larger southern-Istrian household rather than an origin of its own**, and the question is which of the other three it belongs to. The one clue that pointed at Friuli was tested in September 2026 and proved to be a mis-attached record from a Zoppola family of the same name.
families.who: Grgo of Ližnjan, an Antonio in the naval cemetery at Pula, and two who died in France.

families.name: Out of Corsica, to the Caribbean
families.rests: A family history written from inside it: **«LOS FRANCESCHI, la pequeña historia de una familia»**, Napoleón Franceschi González, Caracas 2002. **Pietro Franceschi, 29 June 1694 – 12 February 1771**, then Gasparo (1721–99), Francesco Maria (1750–1828), Pietro (1789–1871) and **Simone, born and dead at Ersa, 1826–1907**, whose son François Marie died at Miranda in Venezuela in 1918. Ninety pages, and **not one line of it touches Istria.**
families.who: A dry, poor cape that never held two thousand people, so they went to sea or they left.

clusters_head: Households of the name that must belong to one of the four, and cannot yet be assigned
clusters_lead: These were being counted as lines. They are not origins; they are real households in real registers whose parent family this archive cannot yet name. Each one is a question with an address.

clusters.what: Kobler, working the civic registers, found three and declined to join them to each other. **Valentino, «venuto dalla Carnia», a citizen in 1739** — almost certainly the Carnian family. **Giovanni Battista, «venuto da Pisino», a citizen in 1746** — almost certainly the same, since «da Pisino» in a Fiume register means the county, and that is where Gologorica is. And an earlier Fiume stock that is nobody's yet.

Kandler's list of the Carnian families settled at Sanvincenti names Defranceschi among Lupieri, Fiorencis, Fabris, Crosilla and the rest. So the origin is Carnian; whether it is *our* Carnian household or another out of the same valley is not settled.

A citizen-class household from before 1772 — Dominus Giovanni Battista, son of Dominus Francesco, marrying Catharina Akačić by dispensation. Styled *Dominus*, which separates them from the peasants on the same page. Which of the four they belong to is open.

**Read, September 2026.** Not a scatter but one family: in the Pula registers from **1667**, then Pula, Fažana, Premantura, Medulin and Barban for three centuries, with Ližnjan as its last address rather than its origin — which means **Ližnjan is not a separate family and should not be counted as one**. Two outliers complicate it: a death at Rovinj in 1728, a baptism at Šterna in 1778. **The one clue that pointed north has been tested and discarded**: the Giambattista with children at Zoppola in Udine is a local man «De Franceschi o Samassa» of a local Zoppola family, attached by Smart Matching — and Zoppola is the Friulian plain, not Carnia. The cluster has no origin yet.

A third and much larger southern presence, and Carlo's own book names Franceschi among the nobles of Pola «venuti da Capodistria» before the plague of 1631 — which would make them the extinct Koper family, not any of the four.

dest_head: Where the name went — and whose name it was
dest_lead: Every destination on the family's old map, with the one thing the map did not say: which family it belongs to, and how well that is known. Half of them are not this family at all, and saying so is the point.

dests.what: Zdravko, Petar, Ivan and Felix in the labour camps and then the displaced-persons files, 1941–51. Named individuals, dated documents.
«Emigré Australie le 8.3.49» on Anton's index card. Zdravko's bronze at Horsham.
Hedviga Blažević died at Johannesburg in 2001; the keeper of this archive was born there.
Not a line — a station. Ivan went home to Senj and is buried there, 1925–1995.
Basilio of Gračišće, born 29 September 1909, and his son Dario born at Gallignana in 1937; Giuseppe born at Gračišće 1892, dead in New York 1940; Albina off the Conte Rosso in 1922.
Acta Croatica counts about sixty people of the name in Croatia today, mostly born at Split or Imotski. That is the Dalmatian family, still there.
Seget's own country. Koper is a title rather than a home: nobles of Capodistria from 1802, while living at Seget.

Grga died at Zagreb and thirteen graves of the name are in the city's cemeteries. **Monheim, corrected**: the pin's coordinates point at Bavaria, but the town that matters is Monheim am Rhein — and the only private listing of «Defranceski» in the whole German directory is five kilometres away at Langenfeld, in the same district. Not proof, and the people are living, so no one is named. But the pin is no longer sourceless.

Rotilio, eighth of the Eleven of Gračišće, is said to have gone to Buenos Aires with two daughters. **Searched properly in September 2026 and not found**: no Rotilio of this surname anywhere in the Argentine record, and the Defranceschi who are there are an Italian-mainland stock. The album's one supporting detail — the name of his wife — turns out to be his sister's marriage. CEMLA's arrival index is behind a bot check and stays unsearched.

dests.place: Brazil — Rio Grande do Sul, Santa Catarina, São Paulo
dests.what: The largest cluster of the surname anywhere, and **not this family**. The in-law names are Marcato, Busatto, Poletta, Raminelli, Barbiero, Negri, Catteri, Facco — every one of them Veneto. This is the Italian colonisation from 1875 out of the Veneto, Friuli and the Valsugana, with a separate São Paulo coffee-belt migration beside it.
Domme De Franceski, born in Italy 1880, at the Penn Iron Mining Company at Norway, Michigan, with a wife born in Switzerland. Nothing joins him to Istria.
Italian-speaking Switzerland, over the border from Lombardy. A different stock of the same ordinary patronymic.

**Now a line of its own on this page.** A Florentine-descended family settled at **Ersa in Cap Corse**, documented from **1694** in Napoleón Franceschi's own history of it, out through Puerto Rico, Saint Thomas, Trinidad and Haiti to Venezuela. It produced a Napoleonic brigadier general, made a baron of the Empire in 1810, and a modern historian of the Revolution. It has nothing to do with Istria, and that is the point of drawing it.
Two born at Barban in 1924 and 1931, dead at Charleville in the Moselle in 2002 and at Cannes in 2016. The Istrian exodus took a road this archive had not recorded.

dests.place: Venezuela · Puerto Rico · Trinidad · St Thomas
dests.what: The Corsican family's own road, out of Ersa through the French and Spanish Caribbean. There is a *Centro de Arte Alejandro Franceschi* at Yauco in Puerto Rico and a village there called **Córcega**. Not this family — and fully documented, which is what makes it useful.

close: So the honest sentence is this. **Five families with an origin in documents, of which four are documented and one — Ližnjan, now folded into southern Istria — has only a place.** **Three of the five are ours or arrived beside ours; one, Corsica, never came near Istria at all and is drawn to show what a parallel line looks like.** Five clusters of real households belong to one of them and cannot yet be told which. And a diaspora in which five destinations are demonstrably ours, four belong to the other families, and the rest are people who share the commonest patronymic in Italy.
source_fam: Assembled September 2026 from this archive's own pages, and restructured after David Defranceski pointed out that it had been adding three different kinds of thing together and calling the total «lines».

svetjoin.heading: Svetvinčenat, 1657–1737 — and the «Pula 1667» that was never Pula
svetjoin.lead: David asked for the people in the roster to be worked through one by one, to see whether any of them join two regions. This is the first result, and it moves a line. It came out of the three earliest people in the roster — born 1669, 1671 and 1674 — by asking the only question that matters about an index entry: **which book is it actually in?**

rows.text:
The index gives the place of these baptisms as «**Croazia, Austria**» — no parish at all, which is why they have sat unplaced. But every FamilySearch index entry carries the ark of the image it was read from, and every image ark resolves to a **DGS film number**. These resolve to **DGS 005497884**, and the catalogue entry for that film reads: «**Matična knjiga, 1568–1917 · Rimokatolička crkva. Župa Svetvinčenat**» — the parish register of **Svetvinčenat**, held by the Croatian State Archive in Zagreb.

So the register is named even though the index is not. **The method is repeatable and it is now the archive's standard practice for any «Croazia, Austria» entry.**

This archive's fourth family opens: «**Pula, 1667** — Anto De Franceschi, with children entered in October 1667 and November 1669 — the earliest of the cluster.» Those are **Franceschina, baptised 23 October 1667**, and **Mattia, born 8 November 1669** — both children of **Anto De Franceschi and Marta**.

They are not Pula entries. **They are Svetvinčenat entries**, forty kilometres north, in a different parish and a different world. The southern-Istrian line's earliest evidence has been standing on a place-name the index never gave it.

rows.lab: And Svetvinčenat is the Carnian colony
rows.text:
That matters because Svetvinčenat is not an unknown. It is the cluster this archive lists as **not placed** — one hundred and forty-two records from 1666 — and three separate authorities call it Carnian. **Kandler** names the Carnian families settled at Sanvincenti. **Doblanović**, reading the Status animarum of 1734, finds the surnames that occur inside the *castello* and nowhere else in the parish — «**De Franceschi, Crosila, Bergamo, Moro, Fiorencis**» — and says they «came from the area of Carnia» and were «mainly in trade». **Brhan** finds a **Stanzia De Franceschi** on the 1820 cadastral map, a farmstead the family had held and already lost.

**So the oldest records of the «origin unknown» line are records of a documented Carnian colony.**

Pulled out of the index and sorted, the parish gives a continuous presence:

**1657** Francesco, son of **Zuanne and Orsola** · **1666** Colotta, daughter of **Nadal and Fiora** · **1666** Fioretta, daughter of **M.ro Batta and Domenica** · **1667** Franceschina and **1674** Mattio, of **Anto and Marta** · **1670** Luca, of **Francesco and Giacoma** · **1671** Giacomo, of **Andrea and Zuana** · **1673** Giovanna and **1688** Zuana, of **Gaspero, with Marietta then Anta** · **1701** Veneranda, of **Gasparo and Antonia** · **1703** Domenica, of **Piero and Vittoria** · **1704** Antonio, of **Mattio and Zuanna** · **1707** Piero, of **Lunardo and Eufemia** · **1709** Maria, of **Nardo and Zuanna** · **1722** Martino, of **Mattio and Elisabetta** · **1733** Maria, of **Giacomo and Anzoletta** · **1734** Pietro and **1735** Bata, of **Nadal and Anta** · **1737** Andrea, of **Vitorio and Francesca**.

That is **at least twelve distinct fathers of this surname in one small town between 1657 and 1737** — and the earliest of them, Zuanne, is **four years before the surname enters the Moncalvo book** and twelve years before the Mione headmen's list.

rows.lab: Two given names that reach out of it
rows.text: **Lunardo — Nardo — Leonardo.** A Leonardo De Franceschi is baptising children at Svetvinčenat in 1707 and 1709. The Gologorica house's own byname is «**detti Leonardi**», and its pedigree carries Leonardus 1697–1773, Leonardus 1766–1848 and Leonardus 1847–1917. Leonardo is not a common name in these registers, and it is now in both places at once. Inferred **Vitorio.** A Vitorio De Franceschi is baptising at Svetvinčenat in 1737 — and Vitorio, Vittorio and Victorius run right through the Pula–Fažana–Medulin group: Vitorio born 1720, Vitorio 1758, Vittorio 1795, Vittorio Giovanni 1849. **Neither is proof.** A shared font-name is the weakest evidence there is, and this archive has said so about better cases than this. What they are is **two threads to pull**, both bounded: the Svetvinčenat register is filmed and readable, and it will say whether these are the same men.

The Lines page draws the fourth family as «**Out of southern Istria — origin unknown**», documented from 1667 at Pula. Two of those three words now need work. The **1667** is right; the **Pula** is wrong; and **«origin unknown» may not survive**, because the register those earliest entries come from is a parish whose De Franceschi are called Carnian by everyone who has studied them.

What this archive will **not** do is redraw the diagram on this. Two of the twelve Svetvinčenat fathers could be the ancestors of the Pula group, or none of them could; the town sat on the road between the county of Pazin and the Pula country and people moved both ways. The lane keeps its dotted origin, the correction to «Pula» is made, and the Svetvinčenat cluster is now the **first place this archive will read page by page** rather than by index.

svetjoin.source_svet: FamilySearch record index, collection 2040054, Croatia church books — personas resolved to image arks, image arks resolved through the digital-archive service to **DGS 005497884**, and that film identified in the FamilySearch catalogue as «Matična knjiga, 1568–1917», Rimokatolička crkva, Župa Svetvinčenat, Hrvatski državni arhiv u Zagrebu (catalogue item koha:728445). Read September 2026. The Carnian identification of the parish is Kandler by way of Carlo De Franceschi's «L'Istria» (1879), Danijela Doblanović on the Status animarum of 1734, and Dean Brhan on the Catasto franceschino of 1820.
